CHAIR ( Senator Marielle Smith ): I declare open this hearing of the Education and Employment Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present, and I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today.

The committee has fixed Friday 24 July 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with corporate and enabling services of the Department of Education. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice.

I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Dr Jess Walsh, Minister for Early Childhood Education and Minister for Youth, who is representing the Minister for Education. Minister, do you have an opening statement?

Senator Walsh: Good morning, Chair. No.

CHAIR: Great. I also welcome Mr Tony Cook PSM, Secretary of the Department of Education. Mr Cook, do you have an opening statement?

Mr Cook : No, Chair, but I would like to congratulate Senator Mulholland on her family news, and I'd also like to just let the committee know that we have graduates in the back row who'll be rotating through the day—so you'll see them come and go—so they can see what the joys and benefits of the Senate estimates process are for them.

CHAIR: Thank you, Mr Cook. Yes, we're very delighted that government numbers on this committee are growing by one. It's excellent news. On behalf of the committee, I'm sure we all extend our warm congratulations to Senator Mulholland. And welcome to the graduates. It's great to have you in the room. I started my career in the APS as a graduate, and it was a wonderful experience, so I hope you get as much out of it as I did, and I hope you learn a lot today. We promise not to call you.

Mr Cook : But I don't!

CHAIR: Be kind to your secretary always! Maybe at the end, if we're getting bored. We'll kick off the questions. Senator Kovacic, you have the call this morning.

Senator KOVACIC: My personal congratulations to Senator Mulholland. I would just like some clarification: with the move of the Office for Youth from the early childcare cluster to the schools cluster, where should questions for the Office for Youth be asked today, and under what program number?

Mr Cook : Schools—so the next bracket, basically, after corporate.

Senator KOVACIC: So schools?

Mr Cook : All in schools, yes.

Senator KOVACIC: And those officials will be there?

Mr Cook : They will be, yes.

Senator KOVACIC: Wonderful. When did that move take effect?

Mr Cook : It happened before the last estimates process. I think I announced it at the previous estimates.

Senator KOVACIC: So it was December?

Mr Cook : Yes.

Senator KOVACIC: That's what I thought too. Just to clarify, how many ASL were in the Office for Youth both before and after the move?

Mr Cook : We may actually have to ask the Office for Youth people to help me with that.

Senator KOVACIC: When they're here? Okay, I'll ask them those.

Mr Markovic : They'll be able to tell you the number, but we moved the entire team. There was no change; it was a move from one group to another.

Senator O'Sullivan interjecting—

Mr Markovic : Yes, there was no change to resourcing; it was simply a move to align responsibilities.

Senator KOVACIC: There was no change to any of the funding or its role?

Mr Markovic : It was literally a move between deputy secretaries.

Senator KOVACIC: I was just curious because the portfolio budget papers have removed the KPIs for the Office for Youth out of the budget papers from last year to this year. Is that for that reason?

Mr Cook : No. We actually reviewed a range of our KPIs, so you'll notice a number of KPIs have changed as a result of that. It was basically work we did with the Audit Office—again, Mr Markovic can probably provide more detail—looking at the KPIs we had and whether those KPIs were effectively assessing the work of the department. That was effectively the reason for that. If you want any more details on the KPI process, Mr Markovic can help us with that.

Mr Markovic : I might invite one of my finance colleagues up just to talk a little bit about the work we've been doing with the Audit Office. But, as the secretary said, we have been focusing on reviewing our KPIs progressively to make sure they best represent measures of performance for the department. Again as the secretary said, we've been responding to feedback from the Audit Office about that. I might just see on the specific measure whether either Mr Boyd or Ms Shrives might be able to help us with some further detail.

Ms Shrives : As part of our process in preparing for the next financial year, we go through a review of all of the performance measures for a range of factors, including meaningfulness, completeness, usefulness and compliance against the PGPA requirements. When we were reviewing the performance measures for the Office for Youth, because there were a range of performance measures within outcome 1.5 there was a decision to actually reduce the number and focus on those that have more meaningfulness to the program as a whole. You'll see, when you look at program 1.5, there are some that now focus on early childhood functions within that particular program and then some focusing more meaningfully on the broader outcomes of 1.5. As part of that process, those two performance measures were reduced. Our intention is still to include some of the information within the annual report but just not have them as a performance measure itself.

Senator KOVACIC: Overall did you find the KPIs were effective for the Office for Youth but you just worked out which were more or less effective?

Ms Shrives : It wasn't a question of effectiveness so much as a better representation of the range of measures within program 1.5. Because the Office for Youth measures were very small and very specific to a very targeted function within the department and because they have their own reporting mechanisms as well through the engage reporting they're supposed to do as part of their strategy, the decision was to streamline and remove some of that duplication of effort and pick up some of those metrics elsewhere in the annual report, part of the year-end review section we're also intending to update, but just not have them also go through the much more rigorous audit process that comes as part of being part of the performance statement. It's not about effectiveness; it's just about the most efficient way to still provide the information but also make sure we're giving the parliament and the reader a better picture of the performance of the program itself.

Mr Cook : You'll see on page 38 of the PBS that the footnote about Office for Youth says that data will still be provided in the annual report and also in the Engage monitoring and evaluation report. The data is not going anywhere, but we've reduced the number of KPIs more broadly across the department, just to clarify that.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you for that explanation. I want to talk a little bit about some staffing arrangements. I have documents 001 and 001A to table. I want to start by asking some questions about staffing arrangements, corporate governance and the like in the department. In the most recent annual report for the 2024-25 financial year, you said you had adopted 'a target to reduce outsourcing expenditure by $30,000 in 2024-25'. In the same report, consultancy expenditure was $14.327 million and non-consultancy contract expenditure was $188.437 million. I'm just curious: why this $30,000 target out of such an extraordinarily large sum? What's the point of actually pointing that out?

Mr Cook : I think that's part of the work we did on the strategic commissioning framework—again, I've got the right people at the table—where departments were asked to set a target about work that may be done external to the department that could be done internal to the department. Despite the size of some of those contracts you just read out, we're a very small user of contractors broadly. I think in the entire department it's something like 84 contractors. We looked at the key functions of the department—there's actually something in the annual report in more detail around that—we identified how much of the key work we could change from being external to internal, and the dollar value we came up with was about $30,000. But, again, Mr Markovic can help me with a bit more detail on that.

Mr Markovic : The secretary has pointed to the strategic commissioning framework. At the heart of that framework is really that a certain set of work should be done by public servants and shouldn't be outsourced. When we went through the assessment process we did identify one arrangement, which was for the sum of $30,000, that should have been performed by public servants according to that framework. At the time, we had an independent chair of our risk committee, so we used an external person to run our risk committee. Against the strategic commissioning framework, the assessment is that that is probably something that should have been led by a public servant, and then we should have had external support. We identified that contract for $30,000 and in the course of the year made the change to our governance arrangements such that that wasn't outsourced any longer.

Senator KOVACIC: It's effectively that one single role.

Mr Markovic : Correct.

Senator KOVACIC: It was weird to me because, under the APSC Strategic Commissioning Framework, there is that target of $30,000 of non-core work, compared with a target of $528 million across the whole Public Service—the outsourcing was $14.3 million. Is the $14.3 million expenditure that went to consultants all non-core work?

Mr Markovic : There are some minor exceptions in there, but predominantly it is the assessment that it's non-core work and is appropriate for outsourcing. When you look at the definition of 'core work' it is things like leadership roles, decision-making—

Senator KOVACIC: Chairing that committee is core because it's a leadership role?

Mr Cook : That's right.

Mr Markovic : SES is another good example. We don't use contractors for SES roles; they're all permanent public servants bound by the Public Service Act. That's the intent of the strategic commissioning framework. It doesn't preclude agencies from engaging contractors and consultants but asks where it is appropriate and where it is not appropriate.

Senator KOVACIC: Just so I've got my understanding clear, the $14.3 million expenditure on non-core work by consultants is correct for outsourcing or outsourced expenditure?

Mr Cook : Just your source for that, to help me again—where you got that number from?

Senator KOVACIC: I'll just have to check that. It's from your annual report. Do you need the page?

Mr Markovic : Page 155. The number in our annual report is correct. It is our consultancy contracts entered into for the period 2024-25.

Senator KOVACIC: Could you tell me how many staff are engaged on labour hire arrangements, and what is the value of those arrangements?

Mr Markovic : We currently have 88. I might correct the record. I think I told the secretary 84 a minute ago; I apologise. We have 88 contractors, which represent 4.6 per cent of our workforce. The year-to-date spend on those contractors as of 31 March is $13,423,804.

Senator KOVACIC: Has the department offered voluntary redundancies in this financial year, and are you planning to do so in the upcoming financial year?

Mr Cook : We offer voluntary redundancies regularly.

Senator KOVACIC: It's an ongoing process?

Mr Cook : VRs is an ongoing process. Staff at any time can ask us for a VR. There might be situations where, as a result of terminating programs or programs finishing, we may make decisions about roles or functions that are no longer required in the department as well. There's a usual process around that. Every year over the last couple of years, I think, we've had some component of voluntary redundancies. In terms of this financial year, I think it's—

Senator KOVACIC: If you could give me the uptake and the cost, that would be great.

Mr Markovic : As at 31 March, we had four voluntary redundancies, and the severance payment for those was $520,689.92.

Senator KOVACIC: Does the department offer secondment arrangements?

Mr Cook : Secondment arrangements?

Senator KOVACIC: Do you second people into other roles?

Mr Cook : Do you mean from other departments or outside?

Senator KOVACIC: Yes, and vice versa.

Mr Markovic : Yes, we will occasionally. We have secondment arrangements both with other APS agencies and on occasion external to our agency as well.

Senator KOVACIC: How do they normally come about? Would the department request them, or do you receive a request by a receiving entity? Is it a bit of both? How are they usually paid for?

Mr Cook : Through a range of ways. Sometimes it's through a surge workforce. Classic examples are things like COVID-19, where Services Australia, for example, might need a surge workforce. Staff get seconded to Services Australia, for example, around some of that work. It really depends on each of the situations. Sometimes the home department will pay for that staff member. Sometimes the seconding department will pay for that staff member if they have a budget around it. It happens around a whole range of different ways. We also have a mobility program where we do a surge in the department itself as well. If I think there's a particular area in the department that requires additional resourcing, we may move staff from other areas to actually meet that surge for that particular time.

Senator KOVACIC: Do you second people out to other agencies as well?

Mr Cook : Yes, when there are requests. Often it's done through an expression-of-interest process that we will put in our own department. For example, again, let's just use COVID-19. There might have been a request from a department for additional staff across the APS to help them with the surge workforce. We would often do an expression-of-interest process in our department for people who are interested in that role, and then they would be seconded to that department to do that work for that period of time.

Senator KOVACIC: Does the department maintain internal committees to deal with audit, governance and probity risk?

Mr Cook : Yes.

Senator KOVACIC: When did those committees last meet?

Mr Cook : The Audit and Risk Committee meets regularly.

Mr Markovic : We'll see if we've got the date. We have an Audit and Risk Committee. We're required to have an audit committee under the PGPA Act, and we have an Audit and Risk Committee. I'll check if we've got the date with us. I'm pretty sure we can find that, but I'll check. I'll invite Ms Murphy.

Ms Murphy : The committee last met in March. I'd have to take the exact date on notice.

Senator KOVACIC: To clarify one piece in relation to the secondments—I note that COVID context, but, in a non-COVID context, is that something that happens regularly? Is it an ongoing kind of thing?

Mr Cook : It is ongoing. To some degree, it's situational—for example, fuel or if something else happened. It really depends on what's happening in the international and national environment to a large degree. But we are always open. We're often approached by other departments, and we sometimes approach other departments as well about secondments. It is a regular thing across the APS.

Senator KOVACIC: In relation to the Audit and Risk Committee meetings, what were the matters that were raised at the last meeting of that committee in general terms?

Mr Cook : Generally, what often happens is I'll go—not to every meeting, but from time to time—as the secretary, and I'll provide the committee with an overview of contextual things that are happening in the department and things that might be impacting on the department from a risk perspective. What will then usually happen is there's a rotating arrangement where a deputy secretary will attend the audit committee and talk about particular items, like child care, schools and higher ed, and any issues that they might have around risks. What then would normally happen is the internal audit team would report on internal audits that have been undertaken and the results of those audits, and they sometimes ask the relevant manager or SES to come and talk to that and what the departmental response has been in relation to those audits as well. Again, I'll ask Ms Murphy for a bit more detail about anything I've missed.

Senator KOVACIC: I'd be interested in any specific things in the most recent meeting.

Ms Murphy : In the meetings they do discuss outcomes of internal audits. I believe that there were three internal audits tabled at the last meeting and any recommendations out of that—

Mr Cook : Do we know what they are? I don't know off the top of my head. Do we know?

Ms Murphy : Unfortunately, I don't have that information with me.

Mr Cook : We can give you that on notice if we need to. The other thing that also happens is the chair of the audit committee then also comes to the executive board of the department, which is effectively chaired by me and all the deputies, and the chair of the audit committee then reports to the executive board the work of the committee and any particular findings or outcomes that we need to be aware of from an executive board perspective. The chair of the audit committee also meets with me after every meeting to give me an overview of the work of the audit committee as well.

Senator KOVACIC: You would then, obviously, discuss broader risk and governance issues as well.

Mr Cook : That's right.

Senator KOVACIC: What kinds of issues in relation to broader risk and governance were discussed at your last meeting?

Mr Cook : I would have discussed the budget, I'm sure—the outcomes of the budget. I would have talked about some of the risks, which won't surprise you. Most secretaries always talk about anything to do with IT platforms and where we might be going with IT platforms, ageing IT platforms and things like that. I can't recall what the internal audits were for this meeting and the discussion, but I get the results of all the internal audits and we have a discussion—I have a discussion with the chair—about the results of those internal audits, particularly if there's anything the department has said where we don't agree with the recommendation. There's nothing that I can recall, certainly in the last few years, where the department hasn't agreed with the recommendation and hasn't agreed to take action in relation to a recommendation.

Mr Markovic : Around risk, the Audit and Risk Committee also has responsibility for looking at the risk frameworks that we have. They'll have a look through risk appetite and tolerance. They'll look at high-level risks. They sort of do the full spectrum over the course of the year of making sure the framework's right, monitoring risks and then, as appropriate, escalating to the executive board any risks that we need to be alert to.

Senator KOVACIC: Wonderful.

Ms Murphy : Senator, I'll just add that I do have the date of that meeting now; that was 19 March.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you. According to AusTender, you currently have 56 open contracts for temporary personnel services, like labour hire, with a total value of some $27.1 million. Why? What is the rationale behind spending $27 million on labour hire?

Mr Markovic : I might start and then invite the CFO. The open contracts relate to the contractors that I spoke about earlier, the ADA. That's for those people. The contracts can be over multiple years, so the contract value you'll see on AusTender might cut across multiple years, which is why it's higher than the number that I gave to you about actual expenditure. For the contract arrangements, we have a competitive process to pick people. We use panel arrangements in the first instance, then we have a competitive process. That's how we are engaging those contracted staff that I spoke about earlier. I'll see if the CFO has anything to add to that.

Mr Boyd : As Mr Markovic was saying, the reason, if you like, for the number of them is for short-term roles or where we need a specialist skill set the department might not have. IT is a good example. There might be times where we're after some specific IT skills and it's better to get them in on a temporary engagement. Another one might be where there's a decision by government where we might need to stand up a program. We might need some short-term skill to help establish that, and then public servants take over those roles.

Senator KOVACIC: To confirm, is the total value of the open contracts on labour hire $27 million, and is that all categorised as non-core work?

Mr Boyd : I don't have that figure in front of me. If it's on AusTender, then that's the figure. But, yes, that is non-core work.

Senator KOVACIC: Could I please table documents 2, 3 and 4. I'm going to ask a couple of questions around each of those individual contracts when you get those. Under contract CN4168277, you're paying $360,000 for a program officer. Under contract CN4170998, you're paying $361,979 for a business analyst. Under contract CN4183268, you're paying $382,003 for a senior change and training specialist. These are each one-year contracts from what I can see. Basically, we have here $1.1 million to engage three staff for one year. Is that accurate? Is my understanding correct?

Mr Boyd : Given these are notices from AusTender, they would be the value that has been undertaken through the procurement—the value of the contract—so that's correct. Without knowing each of these individual ones specifically, I would note that one of the ones you spoke to, CN4170998, relates to a business analyst, for example.

Senator KOVACIC: Yes.

Mr Boyd : That's probably one of the categories I was talking about before, where we might bring in a specialist skill set to work within the department on a particular activity or project. Similarly, with things like the program officer—and we could look to see what part of the department has undertaken this procurement—it could be that example where there's been a decision, we need to get some resources in with skill sets to help us while the department then sets that program up and running—short-term surge skill sets that the department doesn't have.

Senator KOVACIC: But these are all one-year contracts. Do you consider a one-year contract to be a short-term surge?

Mr Boyd : Again, it would depend on the circumstances around each procurement. We'd have to find out the relevant area of the department that—

Senator KOVACIC: I know, but, from a general perspective, what would a short-term surge contract normally be?

Mr Boyd : Again, it depends on the work. We could have a project, for example, that's multi-year, so one year would seem absolutely correct. If you have a three-year project, where government has funded some work for three years or more, that could be an appropriate timeframe. That's why I'm saying it's difficult to draw a generalisation.

Senator KOVACIC: That makes sense. You currently have six contracts open with KPMG with a combined value of $4.1 million, including a contract for taxation support services. There's $2.7 million for independent project assurance services for the Education Funding System project and around $680,000 to advise on 'an initial business case to explore options for the Commonwealth to invest in owning and leasing ECEC centres throughout the Building Early Education Fund'. Is that all correct?

It's about strengthening initial teacher education, and it's also about retaining those in the profession. They're the three core pillars of the action plan. As part of that, the government's invested close to $160 million in additional university places in education. Senator MULHOLLAND: Fantastic. I understand that the ABS data of the last few years shows that there has been an improvement, particularly in student-to-teacher ratios. Could you please outline what the Australian Bureau of Statistics student-to-teacher ratio looks at and refers to.

The lower that number, the more teachers there are in the system. In 2022, we were looking at something like, I think, 13.1 students to a teacher, and now, at a national level, that has dropped in 2025 to 12.8. That's across all sectors. Senator MULHOLLAND: So having more teachers means a lower student-to-teacher ratio.

Senator MULHOLLAND: Okay. That's good news. I will move back to the National Teacher Workforce Action Plan. It's obviously been around for a few years now. What parts of the action plan are ongoing?

Ms Brighton : The enduring components of this are not only more people coming into initial teacher education and becoming teachers but the Commonwealth teaching scholarships continuing through till 2028. The professional development that we have done and the resources that we have developed will remain in place. Our core expectation about that workload reduction fund that I mentioned—jurisdictions have been piloting different initiatives. Our expectation is that, where those pilots are showing impact, they would be embedded in the BAU of a state or territory or non-government system on an ongoing basis.

The other element of the workforce action plan—Ms Watson could talk a bit more about this—is the work we've done about mid-career pathways into education. We have pilots running across a number of higher education providers at the moment, looking at different ways to bring potential teachers into the system and have alternative or innovative ways of allowing them to continue their studies while participating in the learning in schools. Perhaps, Ms Watson, you could just talk a little bit about the High Achieving Teachers Program, the HAT Program.

Ms Watson : Yes, certainly. There are 10 partners who have been engaged to provide the High Achieving Teachers Program: nine are universities and one is TFA. Senator MULHOLLAND: Fantastic. I just want to touch on the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement now. How will those agreements build the teacher workforce? What reforms and targets in the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement are related to that work around teacher workforce?

Ms Brighton : During the work on the National Teacher Workforce Action Plan, we got a lot of insight about what was happening in the profession. As we negotiated the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement, one of the core reform areas was around workforce. Part of the reform is all around building a strong and sustainable workforce, and we've got particular targets embedded into the agreement that we need to meet.
